questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes FP16 from BF16 in the context of quantizing neural networks?
questions.choice_A: FP16 has more mantissa bits and fewer exponent bits than BF16, making FP16 better at representing small relative differences while BF16 covers a wider dynamic range.
questions.choice_B: BF16 has more mantissa bits and fewer exponent bits than FP16, making BF16 better for small relative differences while FP16 covers a wider dynamic range.
questions.choice_C: FP16 and BF16 have identical bit allocation; they differ only by endianness.
questions.choice_D: BF16 uses a sign-magnitude representation while FP16 uses two's complement representation for the mantissa.

questions.question: In fixed-point representations, what does the notation Qm.n most directly specify?
questions.choice_A: The number of sign and exponent bits respectively.
questions.choice_B: The number of integer and fractional bits respectively, defining the fixed binary point position.
questions.choice_C: The total number of bits and the base (radix) respectively.
questions.choice_D: The number of mantissa and guard bits respectively.

questions.question: Which characteristic defines uniform quantization as used in many int8 schemes?
questions.choice_A: Bins of varying widths tuned to the data histogram.
questions.choice_B: A nonlinear mapping based on logarithmic spacing.
questions.choice_C: Equally spaced quantization levels across the representable range.
questions.choice_D: An adaptive scale per input value rather than per tensor or channel.

questions.question: Why might non-uniform quantization be preferred over uniform quantization for certain activation distributions?
questions.choice_A: Because it reduces hardware complexity by avoiding scaling factors.
questions.choice_B: Because it can allocate more levels to high-probability regions of the distribution, reducing perceptual or task-specific error.
questions.choice_C: Because it ensures exact representation of all outliers, eliminating clipping.
questions.choice_D: Because it guarantees lower mean squared error (MSE) for any distribution.

questions.question: In symmetric affine quantization for int8 weights, which choice of zero-point is typical and why?
questions.choice_A: Zero-point is set to 128 to center positive and negative ranges.
questions.choice_B: Zero-point is learned during training to minimize loss.
questions.choice_C: Zero-point is fixed at 0 so that zero maps exactly without bias and the mapping is symmetric around zero.
questions.choice_D: Zero-point is set to match the mean of the tensor for optimal MSE.

questions.question: Asymmetric quantization (with nonzero zero-point) is commonly used for activations because:
questions.choice_A: Activations are strictly symmetric around zero in ReLU networks.
questions.choice_B: It allows the integer range to better cover nonnegative and skewed distributions, reducing clipping or wasted codes.
questions.choice_C: It makes dequantization unnecessary at inference time.
questions.choice_D: It enforces exact preservation of batch normalization statistics.

questions.question: Which statement best contrasts per-tensor and per-channel quantization of weights in a convolution layer?
questions.choice_A: Per-tensor uses one scale per kernel element; per-channel uses one scale for the entire tensor.
questions.choice_B: Per-tensor uses one scale for all output channels; per-channel uses a distinct scale for each output channel/filter.
questions.choice_C: Per-tensor quantization cannot be implemented on GPUs; per-channel can.
questions.choice_D: Per-channel quantization is only applicable to activations, not weights.

questions.question: Why does per-channel weight quantization often yield better accuracy than per-tensor quantization?
questions.choice_A: It increases the number of bits available per value.
questions.choice_B: It removes the need for zero-points.
questions.choice_C: It tailors scales to each filter’s dynamic range, reducing quantization error for channels with smaller variance.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees no clipping for any channel.

questions.question: Which rounding method generally minimizes unbiased quantization error when mapping real values to integers?
questions.choice_A: Round toward zero.
questions.choice_B: Round to nearest (ties to even).
questions.choice_C: Floor for positives, ceil for negatives.
questions.choice_D: Always stochastic rounding to the next higher integer.

questions.question: Clipping during calibration primarily trades off which two effects?
questions.choice_A: Lower latency versus higher throughput.
questions.choice_B: Reduced maximum error versus increased bitwidth.
questions.choice_C: Reduced influence of outliers versus increased quantization resolution in the bulk of the distribution.
questions.choice_D: Lower power consumption versus increased on-chip memory.

questions.question: What is the typical affine mapping used for uniform quantization of a real value x into an int8 code q?
questions.choice_A: $q = \text{clip}(\lfloor x \cdot \text{scale} \rfloor, -128, 127)$
questions.choice_B: $q = \text{clip}(\operatorname{round}(x/\text{scale}) + z_p, q_{\min}, q_{\max})$
questions.choice_C: $q = \operatorname{sign}(x) \cdot \log_2(|x|)$
questions.choice_D: $q = \operatorname{round}(x) - z_p$

questions.question: In evaluating quantization quality, how do MSE and max error differ conceptually?
questions.choice_A: MSE measures worst-case deviation; max error measures average deviation.
questions.choice_B: MSE weights large errors linearly; max error squares errors.
questions.choice_C: MSE averages squared deviations across samples; max error considers only the single largest absolute deviation.
questions.choice_D: They are equivalent when errors are symmetrically distributed.

questions.question: Which statement about quantizing activations versus weights is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Weights are dynamic at inference, but activations are static, so weight quantization is harder.
questions.choice_B: Activations have input-dependent dynamic ranges, so their calibration often needs representative data, whereas weights can be quantized statically.
questions.choice_C: Activations are always symmetric, so symmetric quantization is preferred.
questions.choice_D: Weights must use asymmetric quantization to preserve bias terms.

questions.question: What advantage can stochastic rounding provide in low-precision training or quantization-aware training?
questions.choice_A: It completely eliminates quantization noise.
questions.choice_B: It ensures determinism across runs for exact reproducibility.
questions.choice_C: It makes rounding error unbiased over time, which can stabilize training at very low precision.
questions.choice_D: It increases the effective bitwidth of the accumulator.

questions.question: Why are biases often stored in higher precision (e.g., FP32 or int32) even when weights and activations are int8?
questions.choice_A: Biases have smaller dynamic range than weights, requiring more bits.
questions.choice_B: Bias terms accumulate quantization errors from both weights and activations; higher precision preserves accuracy without large cost due to small parameter count.
questions.choice_C: Integer accumulators cannot add bias values.
questions.choice_D: Biases are not used in convolution layers, only in fully connected layers.

questions.question: When using symmetric int8 quantization with range mapped to [-127, 127], why is -128 often not used for weights?
questions.choice_A: To leave room for special NaN encoding.
questions.choice_B: To make the range odd-sized, enabling a zero-point of 0 and symmetric positive/negative levels around zero.
questions.choice_C: Because hardware cannot represent -128.
questions.choice_D: To ensure exact representation of $\pi$.

questions.question: How does per-channel activation quantization compare to per-tensor activation quantization in common deployment settings?
questions.choice_A: Per-channel activation quantization is rarely supported in hardware due to runtime overhead; per-tensor is more common for activations.
questions.choice_B: Per-channel activation quantization is the default in all mobile NPUs.
questions.choice_C: Per-tensor activation quantization requires learning scales during training.
questions.choice_D: Per-channel activation quantization removes the need for calibration data.

questions.question: Which calibration method is most likely to reduce the effect of rare extreme outliers on the chosen scale for activations?
questions.choice_A: Min-max calibration using the absolute minimum and maximum over the dataset.
questions.choice_B: Percentile-based calibration (e.g., using the 99.9th percentile) to set clipping thresholds.
questions.choice_C: Assuming a fixed range like [-1, 1] for all layers.
questions.choice_D: Setting scale from a single batch’s maximum activation.

questions.question: In uniform affine quantization, what is the primary role of the zero-point z_p?
questions.choice_A: It controls the rounding mode.
questions.choice_B: It shifts the integer grid so that a chosen real value (often zero) maps exactly to an integer code.
questions.choice_C: It scales the dynamic range by a power of two.
questions.choice_D: It encodes the sign bit for negative values.

questions.question: Why are integer accumulators (e.g., int32) commonly used for int8 matrix multiplications in quantized inference?
questions.choice_A: Because int8 multiplication is not supported in hardware.
questions.choice_B: Because accumulation grows in magnitude and bitwidth; int32 accumulators avoid overflow and preserve precision before requantization.
questions.choice_C: Because floating-point accumulators are slower.
questions.choice_D: Because int32 supports subnormal numbers.

questions.question: Which scenario is most likely to benefit from non-uniform (e.g., logarithmic or learned) quantization over uniform int8?
questions.choice_A: Weights with approximately Gaussian distributions and limited outliers.
questions.choice_B: ReLU activations tightly concentrated near zero with a long positive tail where small relative differences near zero matter for performance.
questions.choice_C: Inputs already normalized to exactly [-1, 1] with no outliers.
questions.choice_D: Any tensor where MSE is the only metric of interest.
